chief_complaint: headache, dizziness on VOMS test, memory fog 2 weeks post-hit
hpi_details: A 50-year-old female presents to the clinic with headache, dizziness on voms test, memory fog 2 weeks post-hit. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she might have a slow bleed inside her skull or permanent brain damage from hitting her head two weeks ago.
concerns: She is worried that her lingering dizziness and memory lapses will cause her to make serious mistakes at work and lose her job.
expectations: She hopes to get a CT scan to rule out internal bleeding and a doctor's note excusing her from computer screen work for a few days.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Post-Concussion Syndrome is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

After screening for intracranial-injury warning signs, management uses relative rest for 24–48 hours followed by a symptom-limited, graduated return to daily activities. Consider vestibular rehabilitation for persistent dizziness after an appropriate assessment.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

Key HPI features: A 50-year-old female presents to the clinic with headache, dizziness on voms test, memory fog 2 weeks post-hit. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Post-Concussion Syndrome.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Post-Concussion Syndrome.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue strain without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: worsening severe headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, new focal weakness, or increasing confusion.
management_principles: Screen promptly for red flags requiring emergency evaluation, then use a symptom-limited graduated return to learning, work, and activity.
Consider vestibular rehabilitation for persistent dizziness and refer for symptoms that persist, worsen, or substantially impair function.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

must_ask.say: Can you describe how the hit to your head happened, and did you lose consciousness or have any memory loss?
What do your headaches feel like, and are they made worse by bright lights or looking at screens?
Do you feel dizzy or off-balance when you change position, like standing up quickly?
Have you had trouble concentrating, remembering things, or sleeping since the injury?
Have you had any vomiting, seizures, worsening headache, or weakness since the injury?

history.answer: I bumped my head two weeks ago, and since then I have had a lingering headache, dizziness when moving my eyes, and a cloudy brain.
It started gradually over a couple of days after the hit and has been slowly getting more noticeable rather than coming on all at once.
Two weeks ago I hit my forehead against a hard wooden cabinet door at home; I was dazed for a few seconds but did not pass out.
The headache is present almost every day now, usually a constant dull ache that intensifies when I try to work on my computer.
It is a dull, heavy, tight pressure across my forehead and both temples, usually around a 4 to 5 out of 10 in severity.
It tends to be across both sides of my forehead and temples, and sometimes extends back into the base of my neck.
It builds up through the afternoon as I try to focus or look at screens, rather than waking me up from sleep.
Bright screens, loud environments, fast head turns, and mental effort make it worse, while resting in a quiet, dim room helps take the edge off.
No, I never had flashing lights, zigzag lines, blind spots, or numbness before the headache starts.
I get mild queasiness and lightheadedness when the headache peaks, but I have not actually vomited.
Yes, bright fluorescent lights and loud noises irritate me and worsen the throbbing.
I feel a floating dizziness and off-balance sensation whenever I track moving objects, read quickly, or shift my gaze rapidly.
I feel slightly lightheaded if I stand up too fast, but the room itself does not spin in circles around me.
I feel like my brain is in a fog, where I lose my train of thought easily and take twice as long to finish simple tasks at work.
I have been having trouble falling asleep, and I wake up frequently feeling exhausted and drained the next morning.
No, I have never had any seizures, blackouts, or loss of consciousness at any point.
No, I have had no weakness in my arms or legs, no numbness, and no trouble speaking clearly.
No, my vision has not been blurred or doubled, and I have had no redness or pain in my eyes.
No, no eye tearing, red eyes, runny nose, or drooping eyelids.
No, I have had no fever, chills, neck stiffness, or skin rashes.
No, my temples are not tender to the touch, and I do not have jaw pain when chewing or aching in my shoulders and hips.
I tried over-the-counter acetaminophen once or twice last week, but it barely made a difference so I stopped taking it.
No, nobody else at home has a headache, and we do not use gas heaters or unvented stoves.
I have never had high blood pressure, and I do not take blood thinners or aspirin.
I thought a minor bump on the head would clear up in a couple of days, so now I'm worried there's a slow bleed inside my skull.
I can't look at my computer without feeling dizzy, and I'm terrified I'll make a huge mistake on my accounts at work and get fired.
I really want a brain scan to make sure there's no bleeding in there, and a doctor's note for my boss so I can rest away from screens.
I have always been healthy with no history of chronic medical conditions, migraines, or prior concussions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription medications, regular over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I drink one glass of wine occasionally on weekends, but I have not had any alcohol since the injury.
I work as an office accountant and live with my husband and two teenage children.
There is no family history of migraines, brain aneurysms, or neurological diseases.
My last menstrual period was about three weeks ago, my cycles are regular, and there is no chance I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert and oriented to person, place, and time; mildly slow on complex serial calculations and delayed word recall, but speech is fluent and coherent.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light; extraocular movements are intact without ptosis; funduscopic examination reveals sharp optic disc margins with no papilledema or retinal hemorrhage.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with symmetric facial movements, intact sensation, and normal hearing bilaterally.
Full motor strength, 5/5 in all muscle groups of the bilateral upper and lower extremities with normal muscle bulk and tone.
Intact light touch and pinprick sensation symmetrically across all dermatomes bilaterally.
Biceps, triceps, patellar, and Achilles deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally; plantar responses are flexor bilaterally without Babinski sign.
Normal finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements; steady gait and negative Romberg sign with eyes closed at rest.
Supple neck without nuchal rigidity; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Smooth pursuit and saccades provoke mild dizziness and headache; Dix-Hallpike testing does not elicit positional nystagmus or paroxysmal vertigo.
Mild muscular tenderness over the bilateral suboccipital and upper trapezius regions without midline cervical spine bony tenderness; full active range of motion.
No tenderness over the frontal or maxillary sinuses bilaterally.
